choices: Jenkins on a single EC2 instance
CodePipeline with CodeBuild and CodeDeploy stages
Manual builds from a developer laptop
FTP uploads to production
evidence:
Need: commit -> build -> test ->
deploy to staging -> manual approval
-> deploy to prod. Audit every step.
scenarios.hint: Which managed service chains build, test, and deploy stages with approvals?
scenarios.prompt: Which pipeline design fits?
scenarios.situation: The team needs commit-to-production automation with staging, a manual approval gate, and full auditability.
scenarios.title: Commit to production, safely
scenarios.why: CodePipeline orchestrates the full CI/CD workflow — source, CodeBuild, test, CodeDeploy — with manual approval actions and a complete execution history. Self-managed Jenkins reintroduces server ops; laptop builds and FTP are unauditable anti-patterns.

choices: A manual approval action between staging and production
Auto-deploy to production on every commit
Emailing the team before deploy
Deploying Friday at 5 PM
evidence:
Regulated app. Requirement:
human sign-off with identity recorded
before production deploys.
scenarios.hint: Which CodePipeline action type pauses for a human and records who approved?
scenarios.prompt: What enforces the sign-off?
scenarios.situation: A regulated app requires a recorded human sign-off before any production deploy.
scenarios.title: The gate before production
scenarios.why: A CodePipeline manual approval action pauses the pipeline until an approver acts, recording their identity — satisfying the regulation in the pipeline itself. Auto-deploy skips the gate; emails aren't enforced or recorded in the pipeline.

choices: CodeBuild with a buildspec.yml
A developer's laptop
An EC2 instance with cron
Lambda with 15-min builds
evidence:
Builds: flaky, 'works on my laptop'.
Need: reproducible, versioned,
triggered by pipeline.
scenarios.hint: Which managed build service runs buildspec-defined builds?
scenarios.prompt: What makes builds reproducible?
scenarios.situation: Builds are flaky and 'work on my laptop'; the team needs reproducible, versioned, pipeline-triggered builds.
scenarios.title: Works on my laptop, fails in prod
scenarios.why: CodeBuild runs builds in clean, versioned environments defined by buildspec.yml, triggered by the pipeline — eliminating laptop-specific flakiness. Laptop and cron-EC2 builds aren't reproducible; Lambda's timeout and packaging model don't fit general builds.

choices: Blue/green for Lambda with CodeDeploy
All-at-once Lambda deploys
Manual Lambda console publishes
Rolling EC2 deploys for Lambda
evidence:
Lambda API: 10k rps.
Requirement: shift 10% traffic to
new version, monitor, then all.
scenarios.hint: Which deployment shifts Lambda traffic gradually with automatic rollback on alarms?
scenarios.prompt: Which deployment strategy fits?
scenarios.situation: A high-traffic Lambda needs canary traffic shifting (10%, then all) with monitoring and rollback.
scenarios.title: Canary for Lambda
scenarios.why: CodeDeploy's Lambda blue/green (canary/linear) shifts aliases' traffic gradually and can roll back automatically on CloudWatch alarms. All-at-once maximizes blast radius; console publishes are manual; EC2 rolling doesn't apply to Lambda.

choices: Separate pipelines per environment
One pipeline with parameterized environment stages
Copy-paste the pipeline JSON
One pipeline that deploys to prod only
evidence:
Environments: dev, staging, prod.
Current: 3 divergent pipelines.
scenarios.hint: What's DRY for pipelines across environments?
scenarios.prompt: What unifies the pipelines?
scenarios.situation: Three divergent pipelines serve dev, staging, and prod; changes must be made three times.
scenarios.title: One pipeline, three environments
scenarios.why: One parameterized pipeline with per-environment stages keeps the workflow DRY — the same tested artifact progresses through environments with environment-specific parameters. Divergent pipelines drift; prod-only pipelines skip the safety of staging.

choices: CodeArtifact
A public npm registry only
Vendored tarballs in git
An S3 bucket with no versioning
scenarios.hint: Which managed service hosts private, immutable package versions?
scenarios.prompt: What protects builds from upstream breakage?
scenarios.situation: An upstream package deletion broke builds for 6 hours; the team pulls directly from public registries.
scenarios.title: The package that vanished
scenarios.why: CodeArtifact hosts private package repositories with immutable versions, insulating builds from upstream deletions. Public-only registries reintroduce the risk; vendored tarballs bloat repos; unversioned S3 lacks package semantics.

scenarios.title: From Commit to Prod
scenarios.situation: A team deploys by zipping code on laptops and uploading it to servers. Releases are monthly, error-prone, and nobody can say which commit is running in production.
scenarios.prompt: Which pipeline design fixes this with AWS-native services?
evidence: Source (CodeCommit/GitHub) -> Build (CodeBuild: compile/test/package) -> Deploy (CodeDeploy: EC2/ECS/Lambda). CodePipeline orchestrates stages; artifacts pass between stages via an S3 artifact store.
choices: CodePipeline: source stage from version control, CodeBuild to compile/test/package, CodeDeploy to roll out — every commit traceable, every deploy repeatable, artifacts versioned in S3.
Keep the laptop-zip process but add a shared drive so zips are at least centralized.
CodeBuild alone: build the zip in the cloud, then keep manual uploads for deployment.
CodeDeploy alone pointed at the developers' laptops as deployment targets.
scenarios.why: The pipeline's value is the chain of custody: version-controlled source, automated build/test, automated deployment, with artifacts flowing through versioned stages. Any manual step in the middle breaks traceability and repeatability — the exact properties the team is missing.
scenarios.hint: Where does the current process lose track of 'which commit is live'?

scenarios.title: Blue/Green on the Load Balancer
scenarios.situation: A team runs an ECS service behind an ALB and wants zero-downtime deploys with instant rollback and a live production test of the new version before full cutover.
scenarios.prompt: How should CodeDeploy blue/green be configured?
evidence: CodeDeploy provisions the green task set, registers it with a test listener or target group for validation, then shifts production traffic (all-at-once, linear, or canary), keeping blue until termination wait expires for rollback. CloudWatch alarms can trigger automatic rollback.
choices: CodeDeploy blue/green with a test listener for pre-traffic validation, linear traffic shifting, automatic rollback on CloudWatch alarms, and a termination wait keeping blue available.
Update the ECS task definition in place and restart all tasks simultaneously during low traffic.
Deploy green to a separate ALB and ask users to switch URLs when ready.
Shift 100% of traffic instantly with no test listener — validation happens in staging anyway.
scenarios.why: The blue/green value proposition is validation plus reversibility: the test listener proves green against production traffic before cutover, gradual shifting limits blast radius, alarm-driven rollback is automatic, and the surviving blue environment is the rollback plan. Skipping validation or instant-shifting forfeits exactly those guarantees.
scenarios.hint: If green is broken, how do you get back — and how would you have known before users did?

scenarios.title: The Artifact That Vanished
scenarios.situation: A CodePipeline has source → build → deploy stages, but the deploy stage can't find the build output — each stage re-clones the repo instead of passing artifacts.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct pipeline wiring?
choices: Declare named input/output artifacts per stage (build outputs `BuildArtifact`, deploy consumes it) with the pipeline's artifact S3 bucket — stages pass artifacts, not repo re-clones
Give every stage the repo URL; re-cloning is the artifact mechanism
Merge build and deploy into one stage; fewer stages, fewer problems
Artifacts are automatic; the error is a permissions issue
scenarios.why: CodePipeline stages communicate through versioned input/output artifacts in the pipeline bucket — the build stage's output artifact is the deploy stage's input. Without declared artifacts each action runs in isolation.
scenarios.hint: How does the build's output reach the deploy stage?

scenarios.title: Canary With a Kill Switch
scenarios.situation: A canary deploy shifts 10% traffic to the new version, but there's no automatic rollback — a bad canary needs a human to notice CloudWatch.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct automated canary?
choices: Attach CloudWatch alarms to the CodeDeploy deployment group (auto-rollback on alarm) with lifecycle hooks (BeforeAllowTraffic) running validation — the canary becomes self-reverting on metric breach
Watch the dashboard during deploys; humans are the rollback
Canary without rollback is standard; just shift faster
Use blue/green instead; canary can't auto-roll back
scenarios.why: CodeDeploy supports alarm-driven automatic rollback natively — the deployment group rolls back when attached alarms breach. BeforeAllowTraffic hooks gate traffic shift on validation (e.g. smoke tests). Manual watching doesn't scale and misses 3 AM canaries.
scenarios.hint: What reverts the canary without a human?

choices: Console ClickOps
CloudFormation with nested stacks and change sets
Hardcoded scripts per environment
Manual runbooks
evidence:
200 resources, 4 environments.
Need: reviewable changes,
rollback, drift detection.
scenarios.hint: Which IaC service has change sets and drift detection built in?
scenarios.prompt: Which IaC approach fits?
scenarios.situation: 200 resources across 4 environments need reviewable changes, rollback, and drift detection.
scenarios.title: Infrastructure as actual code
scenarios.why: CloudFormation with nested stacks (modularity) and change sets (preview before apply) plus drift detection meets all requirements natively. ClickOps and hardcoded scripts aren't reviewable or repeatable; runbooks drift.

choices: One giant stack for everything
Nested stacks / modules per component with parameters
A stack per resource
No IaC — use the console
evidence:
Network, data, app layers.
Teams: 3, deploying independently.
Need: reuse + independent updates.
scenarios.hint: What gives you reusable, independently-updatable units?
scenarios.prompt: How should the IaC be structured?
scenarios.situation: Three teams deploy network, data, and app layers independently and want reusable components.
scenarios.title: Modules, not monoliths
scenarios.why: Nested stacks (or registry modules) decompose infrastructure into reusable, independently-updatable units with clear interfaces via parameters/outputs. A giant stack couples everything; per-resource stacks explode overhead.

choices: Systems Manager State Manager / desired-state configuration
SSH scripts run by hand
User data that configures once at boot
Golden images rebuilt monthly by hand
evidence:
Fleet: 500 instances.
Requirement: NTP, agents, and
baseline configs enforced continuously.
scenarios.hint: Which service enforces configuration continuously, not just at boot?
scenarios.prompt: What enforces the baseline continuously?
scenarios.situation: 500 instances need NTP, agents, and baseline configs enforced continuously — not just at launch.
scenarios.title: Configuration that stays configured
scenarios.why: State Manager (Systems Manager) applies associations that continuously enforce desired state, correcting drift. Boot-time user data doesn't fix runtime drift; manual SSH doesn't scale; hand-built images are slow to update.

choices: Baking secrets into AMIs
Parameter Store SecureString with IAM-scoped access per environment
Plaintext in the template
The same password in all environments
evidence:
Templates in git.
Need: per-environment secrets,
no plaintext in repo.
scenarios.hint: Which parameter type encrypts values and integrates with IAM?
scenarios.prompt: How should templates handle secrets?
scenarios.situation: IaC templates in git need per-environment secrets with nothing in plaintext.
scenarios.title: Secrets in the template repo
scenarios.why: Parameter Store SecureString (or Secrets Manager) stores encrypted secrets referenced by templates, with IAM policies scoping access per environment. Plaintext in git leaks; baked AMI secrets can't rotate; one password everywhere maximizes blast radius.

choices: Direct stack updates with no preview
Change sets reviewed before execution
Deleting and recreating the stack
Updating via the console
evidence:
Last update replaced the
production database (data loss).
Need: preview + prevent replacement.
scenarios.hint: Which CloudFormation feature shows you the replacement before it happens?
scenarios.prompt: What prevents the next accidental replacement?
scenarios.situation: A stack update replaced the production database, causing data loss.
scenarios.title: Preview before you apply
scenarios.why: Change sets preview exactly what a stack update will do — including resource replacement — so reviewers catch the database replacement before execution. Direct updates skip the preview; delete/recreate guarantees downtime; console updates are unauditable.

choices: Ignoring drift
CloudFormation drift detection with remediation runbooks
Rebuilding everything weekly
Deleting the stack
evidence:
Someone changed a security group
in the console. Template no longer
matches reality.
scenarios.hint: Which feature compares the stack to actual resource configuration?
scenarios.prompt: What catches and corrects the drift?
scenarios.situation: A console change to a security group made the template diverge from reality.
scenarios.title: The console change nobody logged
scenarios.why: CloudFormation drift detection identifies resources whose actual configuration differs from the template, and remediation runbooks (or re-applying the stack) restore the desired state. Ignoring drift compounds; weekly rebuilds are disruptive; deleting the stack is destructive.

scenarios.title: Infrastructure as Code, Safely
scenarios.situation: An engineer is about to apply a CloudFormation template change to production networking. Last time, a template update unexpectedly replaced a database. The team wants no more surprises.
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe change workflow?
evidence: Change sets preview exactly what a stack update will add, modify, or replace before execution. Drift detection reports resources changed outside the template. DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy control what happens on replacement.
choices: Run a change set first and review every resource marked for replacement; check drift detection for out-of-band changes; require approval before executing the update.
Apply the template directly — CloudFormation never replaces resources unexpectedly.
Edit resources in the console for speed, then update the template later to match.
Delete the stack and recreate it from the new template to guarantee a clean state.
scenarios.why: Change sets turn 'apply and pray' into 'review then apply': replacement actions are visible before anything happens, and drift detection catches the console edits that make templates lie. Deleting production stacks to avoid review is the opposite of safety.
scenarios.hint: What would you want to see before the change touches production?

scenarios.title: Config Drift on the Fleet
scenarios.situation: Over a year, engineers hand-tweaked individual servers: different package versions, stray cron jobs, forgotten config edits. 'It works on prod-3' is now a real sentence. Auditors want uniformity.
scenarios.prompt: How does the team eliminate configuration drift?
evidence: Systems Manager State Manager applies associations (desired-state documents) on a schedule and reports compliance. Immutable AMIs/pipelines rebuild rather than repair. Chef/Puppet/Ansible via SSM provide cross-platform config management.
choices: Define desired state as code and enforce it with State Manager associations (or a config management tool via SSM), rebuilding instances from versioned AMIs instead of hand-editing them.
Document the differences between servers in a wiki and have engineers check it before changes.
SSH into each server monthly and manually reconcile configurations against a checklist.
Freeze all changes permanently; drift cannot happen if nothing ever changes.
scenarios.why: Drift is a process failure, not a knowledge problem: desired-state enforcement continuously converges servers back to the declared configuration, and immutable rebuilds make hand-edits impossible by construction. Wikis and manual reconciliation don't scale and don't enforce; freezing changes freezes the business too.
scenarios.hint: What stops the next engineer from hand-editing prod-3 at 2 AM?

scenarios.title: Change Set or YOLO?
scenarios.situation: A CloudFormation stack update to production will replace the database (the template changed an immutable property). The team updates stacks directly.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct safe-update flow?
choices: Create a change set first (`create-change-set`), review the proposed actions — it flags the replacement — then decide (execute, or fix the template); change sets are the preview gate for stack updates
Update directly; CloudFormation warns before replacing
Set a stack policy after the fact; policies preview changes
Use drift detection instead; it previews updates
scenarios.why: Change sets render the exact create/update/delete/replace plan before execution — the only reliable way to catch a replacement-class change pre-apply. Stack policies *prevent* updates to protected resources; they don't preview. Drift detection compares reality vs template, not future changes.
scenarios.hint: What shows the replacement *before* it happens?

choices: One alarm per instance
Composite alarms + SLO-based burn-rate alerting
No alarms; check dashboards daily
Alarming on every metric
evidence:
3000 alarms/week.
On-call ignores them all.
Real incident missed last Tuesday.
scenarios.hint: What reduces thousands of alarms to a few that actually page?
scenarios.prompt: What fixes the alert fatigue?
scenarios.situation: 3,000 alarms per week; on-call ignores them all and a real incident was missed.
scenarios.title: Three thousand alarms a week
scenarios.why: Composite alarms combine signals into meaningful pages, and SLO burn-rate alerting pages only when the error budget is actually at risk — cutting noise to signal. Per-instance alarms multiply noise; no alarms is blindness; alarming on everything is the current failure.

choices: AWS X-Ray with service maps and trace analytics
CloudWatch Logs alone
Guessing from metrics
VPC Flow Logs
evidence:
Request spans 8 services.
Latency spike: which hop?
Logs exist but aren't correlated.
scenarios.hint: Which service correlates the hops into one trace?
scenarios.prompt: What finds the slow hop?
scenarios.situation: A request spans 8 services; latency spiked and uncorrelated logs can't show which hop is slow.
scenarios.title: Which hop is slow?
scenarios.why: X-Ray traces requests across services into a service map with per-segment timing, pinpointing the slow hop. Uncorrelated logs require manual stitching; metrics show symptoms not paths; Flow Logs show network flows, not app spans.

choices: Each service logs in its own format
Structured JSON logs with correlation IDs shipped to a central store
Logs only on the instances
No logs in production
evidence:
Incident review: couldn't follow
one request across 5 services.
Formats differ per team.
scenarios.hint: What lets you query one request across all services?
scenarios.prompt: What makes cross-service debugging possible?
scenarios.situation: An incident review couldn't follow one request across 5 services with differing log formats.
scenarios.title: Following one request everywhere
scenarios.why: Structured JSON logs with correlation IDs, shipped centrally, let you query a single request's journey across services. Per-team formats block correlation; instance-local logs aren't searchable; no production logs is blindness.

choices: The application tier only
CloudWatch RUM + Synthetics canaries
Pingdom-style external ping only
No user monitoring
evidence:
Backend green, but checkout
fails for Safari users.
Nobody knew for 2 days.
scenarios.hint: Which AWS services watch the real user experience and probe it synthetically?
scenarios.prompt: What catches user-facing breakage the backend misses?
scenarios.situation: Backend metrics were green while checkout failed for Safari users for two days.
scenarios.title: Green backend, broken checkout
scenarios.why: CloudWatch RUM captures real-user experience (including browser-specific failures) and Synthetics canaries continuously probe critical flows — catching what backend metrics miss. Backend-only monitoring is exactly the blind spot; external ping alone lacks depth.

choices: Unlimited log retention
Centralized log archive in S3 with lifecycle policies + Athena for ad-hoc queries
Logs deleted after 7 days
Logs in 12 different accounts with no aggregation
evidence:
Compliance: 1-year log retention.
Need: occasional forensic queries.
Volume: 500 GB/day.
scenarios.hint: Cheap durable storage + serverless SQL = which pattern?
scenarios.prompt: What meets retention and forensic needs affordably?
scenarios.situation: 500 GB/day of logs need 1-year retention with occasional forensic queries.
scenarios.title: A year of logs, queried occasionally
scenarios.why: Archiving to S3 with lifecycle policies gives cheap durable retention, and Athena provides serverless SQL for ad-hoc forensic queries without running infrastructure. Unlimited retention in CloudWatch Logs is expensive; 7-day deletion violates compliance; scattered accounts block investigation.

choices: EC2 detailed monitoring (1-min) + custom high-resolution metrics
Default 5-minute basic monitoring
Monitoring the hypervisor only
No monitoring on batch workers
evidence:
Batch workers die silently.
5-min metrics miss the 2-min
failure spikes.
scenarios.hint: What sees sub-5-minute phenomena?
scenarios.prompt: What catches the short-lived failures?
scenarios.situation: Batch workers die silently; 5-minute metrics miss 2-minute failure spikes.
scenarios.title: The spikes between datapoints
scenarios.why: Detailed (1-minute) monitoring plus high-resolution custom metrics capture short-lived failures that 5-minute basic monitoring averages away. Hypervisor-only metrics miss app state; no monitoring is the current failure.

scenarios.title: One Alarm to Page Them All
scenarios.situation: Five separate alarms (CPU, latency, errors, disk, queue depth) each page independently — the team gets 5 pages for one incident and can't tell the real signal.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct alarming design?
evidence: 4 of 5 pages were symptoms of one root cause
choices: A CloudWatch composite alarm combining the children (e.g. alarm on errors AND latency, suppressed when the deploy-in-progress alarm fires) — one page per incident with the true state; keep component alarms as non-paging tickets
More alarms; finer granularity catches more issues
One mega-alarm on CPU only; CPU predicts everything
Composite alarms can't page; only metric alarms can
scenarios.why: Composite alarms express boolean logic over child alarms — page on the incident (symptom combination), ticket the components. Five independent pages for one root cause is alert fatigue by design; composite alarms (which absolutely can notify) collapse it.
scenarios.hint: How do you page once per incident instead of once per symptom?

choices: Trusting every team to tag
AWS Organizations with SCPs + tag policies
One account for everything
Email reminders about tagging
evidence:
12 accounts, 4 teams.
Need: prevent prod deploys outside
pipeline; enforce cost-center tags.
scenarios.hint: Which mechanism sets guardrails even the admin can't cross?
scenarios.prompt: What enforces the guardrails?
scenarios.situation: Twelve accounts need hard guardrails: no prod deploys outside the pipeline, mandatory cost-center tags.
scenarios.title: Guardrails, not guidelines
scenarios.why: Service Control Policies (SCPs) in Organizations set permission guardrails that apply even to account admins, and tag policies enforce tagging standards. Trust and emails aren't enforcement; one account maximizes blast radius.

choices: IAM users with static keys for CI
OIDC federation from the CI provider to IAM roles
Sharing one deploy key
Long-lived tokens in repo secrets
evidence:
CI deploys to AWS.
Current: static access key in CI secrets,
rotated never, visible to all jobs.
scenarios.hint: Which pattern gives CI temporary credentials with no stored secrets?
scenarios.prompt: What secures the CI-to-AWS trust?
scenarios.situation: CI deploys to AWS with a static access key in CI secrets, never rotated, visible to all jobs.
scenarios.title: CI with no stored secrets
scenarios.why: OIDC federation lets the CI provider assume IAM roles with short-lived credentials — no static keys stored anywhere. Static keys in CI secrets are the current vulnerability; shared keys destroy scoping; repo tokens leak.

choices: Config rules + conformance packs across accounts
Manual spreadsheet audits
Trusting team self-reports
Annual pentest only
evidence:
Standard: encrypted EBS, no public
S3, TLS everywhere. 12 accounts.
Need: continuous verification.
scenarios.hint: Which service continuously evaluates rules and aggregates across accounts?
scenarios.prompt: What verifies the standards continuously?
scenarios.situation: Security standards (encrypted EBS, no public S3, TLS) must be continuously verified across 12 accounts.
scenarios.title: Standards that verify themselves
scenarios.why: Config rules packaged as conformance packs deploy the standard's checks across accounts/regions with aggregated compliance views. Spreadsheets and self-reports don't verify; annual pentests are point-in-time.

choices: Allow all actions in the pipeline role
Pipeline roles scoped with IAM Permissions Boundaries
One admin role for all pipelines
No roles; use root
evidence:
Compromised pipeline deployed
crypto-miners with its admin role.
Blast radius: entire account.
scenarios.hint: Which IAM feature caps what a role can do even if its policies are broad?
scenarios.prompt: What limits the next compromise's blast radius?
scenarios.situation: A compromised pipeline's admin role deployed crypto-miners across the entire account.
scenarios.title: Capping the blast radius
scenarios.why: IAM Permissions Boundaries set the maximum permissions a role can ever have, containing a compromised pipeline even if its attached policies are broad. Admin-for-everything is the current failure; no roles/root are worse.

choices: Each developer manages their own keys
Centralized secrets rotation via Secrets Manager with pipeline integration
Secrets in Slack
One shared password
evidence:
Policy: rotate all deploy secrets
quarterly. Current: manual,
last rotation 18 months ago.
scenarios.hint: Which service automates rotation and integrates with pipelines?
scenarios.prompt: What makes rotation actually happen?
scenarios.situation: Quarterly secret rotation is policy but manual rotation hasn't happened in 18 months.
scenarios.title: Rotation that actually rotates
scenarios.why: Secrets Manager automates rotation schedules and integrates with pipelines/services so rotation happens without heroics. Manual processes are the current failure; Slack/shared passwords are breaches waiting to happen.

choices: No approvals ever
Manual approvals + automated policy checks (e.g., OPA/Config) in the pipeline
Approvals via hallway conversation
Deploying then asking forgiveness
evidence:
Change control: every prod change
needs approval + policy check.
Need: speed AND compliance.
scenarios.hint: What combines human judgment where needed with automated checks everywhere?
scenarios.prompt: What satisfies both speed and control?
scenarios.situation: Every production change needs approval and policy checks, without killing deployment speed.
scenarios.title: Speed with guardrails
scenarios.why: Pipelines with manual approval gates for human judgment plus automated policy-as-code checks give both speed and compliance. No approvals fails audit; hallway approvals aren't recorded; deploy-then-apologize is a career-limiting strategy.

scenarios.title: Pipeline Security
scenarios.situation: A company's CI/CD pipeline uses one shared IAM user with admin rights for all stages, stores database passwords in build scripts, and deploys straight to production on every commit.
scenarios.prompt: What is the hardened pipeline design?
evidence: Each stage assumes a least-privilege IAM role. Secrets live in Secrets Manager/Parameter Store, referenced — never embedded. Artifact buckets are KMS-encrypted. Manual approval gates protect production. CodePipeline/CodeBuild roles need only their stage's permissions.
choices: Per-stage least-privilege IAM roles, secrets pulled from Secrets Manager at runtime, KMS-encrypted artifact store, and a manual approval gate before production.
Keep the admin user but rotate its key monthly; the pipeline needs broad access to be flexible.
Move the passwords to environment variables in the build project — better than scripts.
Add the approval gate but keep shared admin credentials so nothing breaks.
scenarios.why: A pipeline with production access is a production system: least-privilege roles bound each stage's blast radius, secret stores remove credentials from code and logs, encryption protects artifacts at rest, and the approval gate makes production promotion a human decision. Rotating a shared admin key doesn't fix shared admin scope.
scenarios.hint: If the build stage were compromised, what could it reach in each design?

scenarios.title: Thirty Accounts, One Rule
scenarios.situation: The org has 30 AWS accounts. A new rule — 'no public S3 buckets, ever' — must apply everywhere, including future accounts, without per-account clicks.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct multi-account governance?
evidence: AWS Organizations, 30 accounts, new ones monthly
preventive, org-wide, automatic for new accounts
choices: An SCP (Service Control Policy) on the organization root/OUs denying `s3:PutBucketPolicy` with public-read conditions (or the account-level S3 Block Public Access) — SCPs are preventive guardrails inherited by all current and future accounts
A Config rule in each account; detective is enough
IAM policies on every user; identity-level control scales
A Lambda in each account fixing buckets after creation
scenarios.why: SCPs set permission boundaries across the org — preventive, inherited, and automatic for new accounts in the OU. Config rules are detective (find after the fact); per-account Lambdas are 30 things to maintain. S3 Block Public Access at the account level complements the SCP.
scenarios.hint: Which control is preventive, inherited, and covers future accounts?

choices: A runbook-driven response: CloudWatch alarm -> SNS -> Lambda/SSM automation -> OpsCenter OpsItem
Waiting for users to report
SSHing into prod to poke around
Restarting everything blindly
evidence:
Incident: 2 AM, disk full on fleet.
Need: detect, respond, track,
learn — repeatably.
scenarios.hint: Which pattern detects, responds, tracks, and learns as a system?
scenarios.prompt: What makes the 2 AM response repeatable?
scenarios.situation: A 2 AM disk-full incident needs detection, response, tracking, and learning — repeatably.
scenarios.title: The 2 AM runbook
scenarios.why: Alarm → SNS → automated remediation (Lambda/SSM) → OpsCenter OpsItem gives detection, response, tracking, and a record for the postmortem — the full incident loop. User reports are slow; ad-hoc SSH is unrepeatable; blind restarts skip diagnosis.

choices: Deleting the compromised instance immediately
Isolating with security groups, snapshotting for forensics, then eradicating
Ignoring it until business hours
Paying the ransom (if ransomware)
evidence:
GuardDuty: instance mining crypto,
talking to known C2.
scenarios.hint: Contain first, preserve evidence, then eradicate — which option does that?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response sequence?
scenarios.situation: GuardDuty flags an instance mining crypto and talking to known command-and-control.
scenarios.title: Containing the compromise
scenarios.why: Isolate (security group quarantine) to stop spread, snapshot for forensics, then eradicate — the contain→investigate→eradicate sequence. Immediate deletion destroys evidence; waiting lets it spread; paying ransoms is never the answer.

choices: A wiki page nobody updates
SSM Incident Manager with response plans, runbooks, and post-incident analysis
A group chat
Phone calls only
evidence:
Last SEV-1: 3 teams, no clear owner,
45 min to coordinate, no record
of decisions.
scenarios.hint: Which service provides response plans, paging, and decision tracking?
scenarios.prompt: What fixes the coordination chaos?
scenarios.situation: The last SEV-1 had no clear owner, 45 minutes of coordination chaos, and no decision record.
scenarios.title: Coordinating the SEV-1
scenarios.why: SSM Incident Manager provides response plans (who does what), automated paging, runbook execution, and a timeline of decisions — plus post-incident analysis. Wikis go stale; chats lose decisions; phone-only leaves no record.

choices: Restarting the service and hoping
Automated rollback on CloudWatch alarms via CodeDeploy
Manual rollback next business day
Leaving the bad deploy in place
evidence:
Deploy caused 5xx spike.
Detected in 3 min by alarms.
Rollback took 90 min (manual).
scenarios.hint: Which deployment feature rolls back automatically when alarms fire?
scenarios.prompt: What shrinks the 90-minute rollback?
scenarios.situation: A bad deploy spiked 5xx errors; alarms fired in 3 minutes but manual rollback took 90.
scenarios.title: Ninety minutes of 5xx
scenarios.why: CodeDeploy's automatic rollback on CloudWatch alarms reverts the deployment within minutes of detection — the detection-to-recovery loop automated. Hope isn't a strategy; next-business-day is 12 hours of errors; leaving it is negligence.

choices: Blameless postmortems with tracked action items
Blaming the on-call engineer
Skipping the review ('we fixed it')
A postmortem that nobody reads
evidence:
Same outage 3rd time this quarter.
Previous 'reviews' named no
causes and tracked nothing.
scenarios.hint: What turns an outage into a fix that sticks?
scenarios.prompt: What breaks the repeat-outage cycle?
scenarios.situation: The same outage happened a third time; previous reviews named no causes and tracked nothing.
scenarios.title: The third time this quarter
scenarios.why: Blameless postmortems that identify systemic causes and track action items to completion are what prevent recurrence. Blame suppresses honesty; skipping review guarantees repeats; unread postmortems change nothing.

choices: One person with all the knowledge
GameDays / fault-injection drills (e.g., FIS) with practiced runbooks
Hoping incidents don't happen
Reading about incidents
evidence:
Team has never handled a real
incident. Runbooks untested.
On-call starts next month.
scenarios.hint: Which practice rehearses failure before it counts?
scenarios.prompt: How does the team get ready?
scenarios.situation: The team has never handled a real incident; runbooks are untested; on-call starts next month.
scenarios.title: Rehearsing the fire
scenarios.why: GameDays and fault-injection (AWS Fault Injection Simulator) rehearse failure modes with the team practicing real runbooks — building muscle memory before it counts. Single points of knowledge, hope, and theory don't prepare anyone.

scenarios.title: The 2 AM Rollback
scenarios.situation: A deployment succeeds technically but error rates spike 20 minutes later — a bad query only visible under production load. The team debates whether to roll forward with a fix or roll back.
scenarios.prompt: What should the deployment system have done automatically, and what is the right call now?
evidence: CodeDeploy supports automatic rollback triggered by CloudWatch alarms or failed lifecycle events. Rolling back a known-good artifact is usually faster and safer than rolling forward an untested fix under pressure.
choices: The pipeline should have had alarm-based automatic rollback wired to error-rate metrics; now, roll back to the last known-good artifact immediately, then fix forward calmly.
Roll forward with a hotfix directly in production — rolling back loses the new features users want.
Wait and watch: error rates sometimes settle on their own after caches warm up.
Manually edit the bad query on each production server to stop the bleeding.
scenarios.why: Automatic rollback on production-health alarms converts a 2 AM judgment call into a pre-decided response; when it wasn't wired up, the disciplined move is still rollback-first because the known-good artifact is the only thing proven at production load. Hotfixes under pressure and manual server edits create new unknowns exactly when unknowns are most dangerous.
scenarios.hint: Which option returns the system to a state that was already proven in production?

choices: Backup and restore
Pilot light
Warm standby
Multi-site active-active with Route 53
evidence:
RTO: near-zero. RPO: near-zero.
Budget: high. Workload: global
checkout.
scenarios.hint: Near-zero RTO/RPO with a high budget — which DR tier is the top one?
scenarios.prompt: Which DR strategy fits?
scenarios.situation: Global checkout needs near-zero RTO and RPO with a high budget.
scenarios.title: Near-zero everything
scenarios.why: Multi-site active-active with Route 53 routing serves traffic from multiple regions simultaneously — near-zero RTO/RPO by design, at the highest cost. The lower tiers (backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby) trade recovery speed for cost and can't hit near-zero.

choices: Route 53 failover routing with health checks
Manual DNS edits
A single region with bigger instances
Email notification to fail over
evidence:
Need: automatic traffic shift
on regional failure. RTO: minutes.
scenarios.hint: Which Route 53 feature shifts traffic automatically on health-check failure?
scenarios.prompt: What automates the traffic shift?
scenarios.situation: Traffic must shift automatically on regional failure with minutes-level RTO.
scenarios.title: Traffic that moves itself
scenarios.why: Route 53 failover routing with health checks detects the failure and shifts DNS automatically. Manual DNS edits can't hit minutes-level RTO; bigger single-region instances share the region's fate; email isn't automation.

choices: Application-level retries only
SQS with visibility timeout + DLQ between tiers
Synchronous chains with no buffering
Hoping downstream recovers fast
evidence:
Payment service slow ->
checkout threads exhausted ->
full outage. Cascading failure.
scenarios.hint: What breaks the synchronous coupling that cascades failures?
scenarios.prompt: What stops the cascade?
scenarios.situation: A slow payment service exhausted checkout threads — a classic cascading failure.
scenarios.title: Stopping the cascade
scenarios.why: A queue between tiers with visibility timeout (redelivery) and DLQ (poison isolation) decouples the services so one slow dependency can't exhaust the other's threads. Retries alone amplify the load; synchronous chains are the failure mode; hope isn't engineering.

choices: Deploying to all AZs at once
Cell-based architecture (shuffle sharding) to bound blast radius
One big database
A single deploy pipeline
evidence:
One bad config took down
all customers at once.
scenarios.hint: Which architecture limits any failure to a fraction of customers?
scenarios.prompt: What bounds the blast radius?
scenarios.situation: One bad config took down all customers simultaneously.
scenarios.title: Blast radius: everyone
scenarios.why: Cell-based architecture (shuffle sharding) partitions customers into independent cells so a bad config or failure affects only a fraction. All-at-once deploys maximize blast radius; one big database is a single point of failure.

choices: Regular restore testing (game days for backups)
Assuming backups work
Testing once a year
No backups; rely on replication
evidence:
Restore needed. Backup corrupt.
Last successful restore test: never.
scenarios.hint: When is a backup actually a backup?
scenarios.prompt: What would have caught the corrupt backup?
scenarios.situation: A restore was needed; the backup was corrupt; a restore had never been tested.
scenarios.title: The backup that wasn't
scenarios.why: Regular restore testing proves backups actually work — an untested backup is just a hope. Assuming, annual testing, or relying on replication (which replicates corruption too) all fail the same way.

choices: RPO 24h / RTO 24h for everything
Tiered RTO/RPO by workload criticality, tested regularly
RPO 0 for everything regardless of cost
No defined RTO/RPO
evidence:
50 workloads. One DR plan.
Critical checkout treated the
same as the internal wiki.
scenarios.hint: Should the wiki and the checkout share a recovery target?
scenarios.prompt: What fixes the one-size-fits-all DR plan?
scenarios.situation: 50 workloads share one DR plan; critical checkout gets the same recovery target as the internal wiki.
scenarios.title: Not everything is tier one
scenarios.why: Tiered RTO/RPO by workload criticality focuses budget and effort where they matter, with regular testing per tier. One-size-fits-all either overspends on the wiki or underserves checkout; RPO-0-everywhere is unaffordable; undefined targets are unplannable.

scenarios.title: The Instance That Heals Itself
scenarios.situation: Compromised EC2 instances must be isolated automatically: detect GuardDuty finding → quarantine the instance (strip security groups) → snapshot for forensics → notify.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct event-driven design?
evidence: finding → isolate → snapshot → notify, no human in loop
choices: EventBridge rule matching the GuardDuty finding event → Lambda/SSM Automation runbook: revoke security-group rules (attach quarantine SG), create EBS snapshots, publish to SNS — event-driven remediation in minutes
A cron job polling GuardDuty every hour; polling is simpler
Manually isolate; automation risks quarantining the wrong instance
Security groups can't be changed on running instances
scenarios.why: EventBridge routes AWS service events to targets in near-real-time — the standard incident-response automation fabric (finding → rule → SSM Automation/Lambda → quarantine + snapshot + notify). Polling adds up to an hour of dwell time; SGs are mutable on running instances by design.
scenarios.hint: What reacts to the finding in seconds without polling?

lessons.title: SDLC Automation — Core concepts
concepts: CodePipeline orchestrates the full CI/CD workflow — source, CodeBuild, test, CodeDeploy — with manual approval actions and a complete execution history. A CodePipeline manual approval action pauses the pipeline until an approver acts, recording their identity — satisfying the regulation in the pipeline itself.
Manual approvals: all-at-once maximizes blast radius; console publishes are manual; EC2 rolling doesn't apply to Lambda.
CodeBuild runs builds in clean, versioned environments defined by buildspec.yml, triggered by the pipeline — eliminating laptop-specific flakiness.

Reproducible builds: laptop and cron-EC2 builds aren't reproducible; Lambda's timeout and packaging model don't fit general builds. CodeArtifact hosts private package repositories with immutable versions, insulating builds from upstream deletions.

example.code:
Environments: dev, staging, prod.
Current: 3 divergent pipelines.
example.walkthrough: One parameterized pipeline with per-environment stages keeps the workflow DRY — the same tested artifact progresses through environments with environment-specific parameters. Divergent pipelines drift; prod-only pipelines skip the safety of staging.

pitfalls: Common trap: manual builds from a developer laptop.
Common trap: manual Lambda console publishes.
Common trap: one pipeline with parameterized environment stages.
Common trap: rolling EC2 deploys for Lambda.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: IaC & Config Management — Core concepts
concepts: CloudFormation with nested stacks (modularity) and change sets (preview before apply) plus drift detection meets all requirements natively. CloudFormation drift detection identifies resources whose actual configuration differs from the template, and remediation runbooks (or re-applying the stack) restore the desired state.
IaC at scale: boot-time user data doesn't fix runtime drift; manual SSH doesn't scale; hand-built images are slow to update.
Nested stacks (or registry modules) decompose infrastructure into reusable, independently-updatable units with clear interfaces via parameters/outputs.

State Manager (Systems Manager) applies associations that continuously enforce desired state, correcting drift. Parameter Store SecureString (or Secrets Manager) stores encrypted secrets referenced by templates, with IAM policies scoping access per environment.

example.code:
200 resources, 4 environments.
Need: reviewable changes,
rollback, drift detection.
example.walkthrough: CloudFormation with nested stacks (modularity) and change sets (preview before apply) plus drift detection meets all requirements natively. ClickOps and hardcoded scripts aren't reviewable or repeatable; runbooks drift.

pitfalls: Common trap: cloudFormation with nested stacks and change sets.
Common trap: cloudFormation drift detection with remediation runbooks.
Common trap: parameter Store SecureString with IAM-scoped access per environment.
Common trap: direct stack updates with no preview.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Monitoring & Logging — Core concepts
concepts: Composite alarms combine signals into meaningful pages, and SLO burn-rate alerting pages only when the error budget is actually at risk — cutting noise to signal.
X-Ray traces requests across services into a service map with per-segment timing, pinpointing the slow hop.
Structured JSON logs with correlation IDs, shipped centrally, let you query a single request's journey across services.
Correlation IDs: per-team formats block correlation; instance-local logs aren't searchable; no production logs is blindness.

example.code:
Compliance: 1-year log retention.
Need: occasional forensic queries.
Volume: 500 GB/day.
example.walkthrough: Archiving to S3 with lifecycle policies gives cheap durable retention, and Athena provides serverless SQL for ad-hoc forensic queries without running infrastructure. Unlimited retention in CloudWatch Logs is expensive; 7-day deletion violates compliance; scattered accounts block investigation.

pitfalls: Common trap: structured JSON logs with correlation IDs shipped to a central store.
Common trap: centralized log archive in S3 with lifecycle policies + Athena for ad-hoc queries.
Common trap: no alarms; check dashboards daily.
Common trap: default 5-minute basic monitoring.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Policies & Standards — Core concepts
concepts: SCPs: service Control Policies (SCPs) in Organizations set permission guardrails that apply even to account admins, and tag policies enforce tagging standards.
OIDC federation lets the CI provider assume IAM roles with short-lived credentials — no static keys stored anywhere.
Config rules packaged as conformance packs deploy the standard's checks across accounts/regions with aggregated compliance views.
Permissions boundaries: IAM Permissions Boundaries set the maximum permissions a role can ever have, containing a compromised pipeline even if its attached policies are broad.

example.code:
Policy: rotate all deploy secrets
quarterly. Current: manual,
last rotation 18 months ago.
example.walkthrough: Secrets Manager automates rotation schedules and integrates with pipelines/services so rotation happens without heroics. Manual processes are the current failure; Slack/shared passwords are breaches waiting to happen.

pitfalls: Common trap: AWS Organizations with SCPs + tag policies.
Common trap: pipeline roles scoped with IAM Permissions Boundaries.
Common trap: manual approvals + automated policy checks (e.g., OPA/Config) in the pipeline.
Common trap: long-lived tokens in repo secrets.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Incident Response — Core concepts
concepts: Incident automation: alarm → SNS → automated remediation (Lambda/SSM) → OpsCenter OpsItem gives detection, response, tracking, and a record for the postmortem — the full incident loop.
Principle: user reports are slow; ad-hoc SSH is unrepeatable; blind restarts skip diagnosis.
Principle: isolate (security group quarantine) to stop spread, snapshot for forensics, then eradicate — the contain→investigate→eradicate sequence.

example.code:
GuardDuty: instance mining crypto,
talking to known C2.
example.walkthrough: Isolate (security group quarantine) to stop spread, snapshot for forensics, then eradicate — the contain→investigate→eradicate sequence. Immediate deletion destroys evidence; waiting lets it spread; paying ransoms is never the answer.

pitfalls: Common trap: SSM Incident Manager with response plans, runbooks, and post-incident analysis.
Common trap: automated rollback on CloudWatch alarms via CodeDeploy.
Common trap: manual rollback next business day.
Common trap: sSHing into prod to poke around.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: High Availability & Recovery — Core concepts
concepts: DR tiers: the lower tiers (backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby) trade recovery speed for cost and can't hit near-zero. A queue between tiers with visibility timeout (redelivery) and DLQ (poison isolation) decouples the services so one slow dependency can't exhaust the other's threads.
Active-active: multi-site active-active with Route 53 routing serves traffic from multiple regions simultaneously — near-zero RTO/RPO by design, at the highest cost.
Route 53 failover routing with health checks detects the failure and shifts DNS automatically.
Cell-based architecture (shuffle sharding) partitions customers into independent cells so a bad config or failure affects only a fraction.

example.code:
Restore needed. Backup corrupt.
Last successful restore test: never.
example.walkthrough: Regular restore testing proves backups actually work — an untested backup is just a hope. Assuming, annual testing, or relying on replication (which replicates corruption too) all fail the same way.

pitfalls: Common trap: cell-based architecture (shuffle sharding) to bound blast radius.
Common trap: a single region with bigger instances.
Common trap: hoping downstream recovers fast.
Common trap: RPO 0 for everything regardless of cost.

simulations.title: Wire up the pipeline
simulations.brief: The team is automating releases for the first time. Order the pipeline stages so each one feeds the next.

steps.context: CI/CD pipeline: from commit to production.
items: Deploy to production with approval gate
Build the artifact and run unit tests
Commit triggers the pipeline
Deploy to staging and run integration tests
Static analysis and security scan

simulations.debrief: You ordered the classic pipeline: commit, build and test, scan, stage, then gated production. Quality gates belong before production, never after.

simulations.title: The red pipeline
simulations.brief: The pipeline is red and the team is blocked. The build log's last lines are your only evidence — read them before you click anything.

steps.symptom: Pipeline fails at the deploy stage; build and test stages are green.
evidence:
Uploading build v4 to s3://ilb-artifacts ... OK
Targeting instances: i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60718 ... OK
ERROR: InvalidInstanceID.NotFound for i-0f9e8d7c6b5a43210
Deploy aborted.
options: Re-run the pipeline — transient AWS errors happen
Fix the deploy target list: it references an instance id that does not exist
Roll back to build v3 — v4 must be broken
Increase the deploy timeout and re-run
steps.explain: The log names the failure precisely: an instance id in the target list does not exist. Green build plus a NotFound at deploy means bad targeting, not a bad artifact — re-running changes nothing.

steps.symptom: The stale id belonged to a terminated host still listed in the deploy config.
evidence:
i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60718  ilb-web-01  running  t3.medium  us-east-1a
i-0f9e8d7c6b5a43210  ilb-db-01   stopped  r6g.large  us-east-1b
options: Remove the dead id from the deploy config and re-run
Terminate ilb-db-01 so the ids match again
Disable the deploy stage until someone investigates
Pin the pipeline to build v3 permanently
steps.explain: Remove the stale target and re-run — the fleet and the artifact are both healthy. This is also why deploy targets should be discovered (tags, ASG) rather than hardcoded.

simulations.debrief: You read the log before acting and fixed the target list instead of the artifact. Most 'broken pipeline' pages are broken config, not broken code.

simulations.title: Make the rollback call
simulations.brief: Production is degraded 20 minutes after a deploy. You are the release captain. The decision tree is yours — choose like the blast radius depends on it.

steps.text: Error rate is 8% and climbing on the new build; the old build was clean. First move?

choices.label: Roll back now — restore the known-good build
choices.feedback: Correct. With a clean previous build and climbing errors, rollback is the fastest mitigation.

choices.label: Roll forward with a hotfix — the team is already debugging
choices.feedback: Rolling forward on a climbing error rate gambles with users. Mitigate first.

steps.text: The hotfix will take 40 minutes; errors hit 15%. Reconsider:

choices.label: Roll back now
choices.feedback: Right — a 40-minute fix window on climbing errors is not a plan, it is hope.

steps.text: Rollback complete, errors back to baseline. What closes out the incident properly?

choices.label: Declare victory and move on — service is healthy
choices.feedback: Skipping the postmortem guarantees a repeat. Healthy now is not the same as fixed.

choices.label: Freeze deploys, run a blameless postmortem, add a canary stage
choices.feedback: Correct — the incident is not over at mitigation. Learn, then harden the pipeline.

simulations.debrief: You made the release-captain calls: rollback beats hotfix on climbing errors, and the incident ends with learning, not just recovery.

simulations.title: The buildspec that lies
simulations.brief: A pipeline keeps 'succeeding' while shipping untested builds. Review this buildspec and click the lines that let bad builds through.

steps.config:
version: 0.2
phases:
  build:
    commands:
      - echo building...
      - npm run test || true
      - npm run package
artifacts:
  files:
    - '**/*'

issues.description: 'npm run test || true' swallows test failures — the build stays green with broken tests.
issues.fix: Remove '|| true' so a failing test suite fails the build.

issues.description: Artifacts include '**/*' — node_modules and secrets can ship to production.
issues.fix: List only the packaged output (e.g. dist/**) in the artifacts files.

simulations.debrief: You caught the two silent-failure patterns: swallowed test results and over-broad artifacts. A green pipeline that ships untested code is worse than a red one.

consoleSims.title: Add the staging gate
consoleSims.brief: The pipeline deploys straight from build to production. Insert a staging stage with an approval gate before production.

tasks.instruction: Create a pipeline stage named staging that consumes the build artifact.
tasks.hint: Add a new stage after build and wire it to the build artifact.

tasks.instruction: Require manual approval before the production stage runs.
tasks.hint: Find the production stage settings and switch approval to manual.

consoleSims.debrief: You added the missing safety: every production deploy now passes through staging and a human gate.

consoleSims.title: Role for the pipeline
consoleSims.brief: The pipeline currently uses deploy-bot's long-lived key. Replace it with an assumable role scoped to deployments.

tasks.instruction: Create a role named ilb-pipeline-deploy that the CI service can assume.
tasks.hint: Create a role (not a user) trusted by the CI service.

tasks.instruction: Scope the role to deploy actions on the artifact bucket only.
tasks.hint: Attach the narrowest deploy policy — PutObject on the artifact bucket, nothing more.

consoleSims.debrief: You removed the long-lived key from the pipeline's blast radius and replaced it with a scoped, assumable role.

terminalMissions.brief: A pipeline can only deploy what exists. List the staged builds.

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `aws s3 ls s3://ilb-artifacts`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly and that the output contains "bootcamp-v3.zip".

cheatsheet.title: AWS DevOps Engineer Professional — Cheat Sheet

sections.heading: SDLC Automation
items: CodePipeline orchestrates the full CI/CD workflow — source, CodeBuild, test, CodeDeploy — with manual approval actions and a complete execution history. A CodePipeline manual approval action pauses the pipeline until an approver acts, recording their identity — satisfying the regulation in the pipeline itself.
Manual approvals — all-at-once maximizes blast radius; console publishes are manual; EC2 rolling doesn't apply to Lambda.
CodeBuild — CodeBuild runs builds in clean, versioned environments defined by buildspec.yml, triggered by the pipeline — eliminating laptop-specific flakiness.

Reproducible builds — laptop and cron-EC2 builds aren't reproducible; Lambda's timeout and packaging model don't fit general builds. CodeArtifact hosts private package repositories with immutable versions, insulating builds from upstream deletions.
Common trap — manual builds from a developer laptop.
Common trap — manual Lambda console publishes.
Common trap — one pipeline with parameterized environment stages.
Common trap — rolling EC2 deploys for Lambda.

One — One parameterized pipeline with per-environment stages keeps the workflow DRY — the same tested artifact progresses through environments with environment-specific parameters. Divergent pipelines drift; prod-only pipelines skip the safety of staging.

sections.heading: IaC & Config Management
items: CloudFormation — CloudFormation with nested stacks (modularity) and change sets (preview before apply) plus drift detection meets all requirements natively. CloudFormation drift detection identifies resources whose actual configuration differs from the template, and remedia…
IaC at scale — boot-time user data doesn't fix runtime drift; manual SSH doesn't scale; hand-built images are slow to update.
Nested — Nested stacks (or registry modules) decompose infrastructure into reusable, independently-updatable units with clear interfaces via parameters/outputs.

State Manager — State Manager (Systems Manager) applies associations that continuously enforce desired state, correcting drift. Parameter Store SecureString (or Secrets Manager) stores encrypted secrets referenced by templates, with IAM policies scoping access per environm…
Common trap — cloudFormation with nested stacks and change sets.
Common trap — cloudFormation drift detection with remediation runbooks.
Common trap — parameter Store SecureString with IAM-scoped access per environment.
Common trap — direct stack updates with no preview.

CloudFormation — CloudFormation with nested stacks (modularity) and change sets (preview before apply) plus drift detection meets all requirements natively. ClickOps and hardcoded scripts aren't reviewable or repeatable; runbooks drift.

sections.heading: Monitoring & Logging
items: Composite — Composite alarms combine signals into meaningful pages, and SLO burn-rate alerting pages only when the error budget is actually at risk — cutting noise to signal.
X-Ray — X-Ray traces requests across services into a service map with per-segment timing, pinpointing the slow hop.
Structured JSON — Structured JSON logs with correlation IDs, shipped centrally, let you query a single request's journey across services.
Correlation IDs — per-team formats block correlation; instance-local logs aren't searchable; no production logs is blindness.
Common trap — structured JSON logs with correlation IDs shipped to a central store.
Common trap — centralized log archive in S3 with lifecycle policies + Athena for ad-hoc queries.
Common trap — no alarms; check dashboards daily.
Common trap — default 5-minute basic monitoring.

Archiving — Archiving to S3 with lifecycle policies gives cheap durable retention, and Athena provides serverless SQL for ad-hoc forensic queries without running infrastructure. Unlimited retention in CloudWatch Logs is expensive; 7-day deletion violates compliance; sc…

sections.heading: Policies & Standards
items: SCPs — service Control Policies (SCPs) in Organizations set permission guardrails that apply even to account admins, and tag policies enforce tagging standards.
OIDC — OIDC federation lets the CI provider assume IAM roles with short-lived credentials — no static keys stored anywhere.
Config — Config rules packaged as conformance packs deploy the standard's checks across accounts/regions with aggregated compliance views.
Permissions boundaries — IAM Permissions Boundaries set the maximum permissions a role can ever have, containing a compromised pipeline even if its attached policies are broad.
Common trap — AWS Organizations with SCPs + tag policies.
Common trap — pipeline roles scoped with IAM Permissions Boundaries.
Common trap — manual approvals + automated policy checks (e.g., OPA/Config) in the pipeline.
Common trap — long-lived tokens in repo secrets.

Secrets Manager — Secrets Manager automates rotation schedules and integrates with pipelines/services so rotation happens without heroics. Manual processes are the current failure; Slack/shared passwords are breaches waiting to happen.

sections.heading: Incident Response
items: Incident automation — alarm → SNS → automated remediation (Lambda/SSM) → OpsCenter OpsItem gives detection, response, tracking, and a record for the postmortem — the full incident loop.
Principle — user reports are slow; ad-hoc SSH is unrepeatable; blind restarts skip diagnosis.
Principle — isolate (security group quarantine) to stop spread, snapshot for forensics, then eradicate — the contain→investigate→eradicate sequence.
Common trap — SSM Incident Manager with response plans, runbooks, and post-incident analysis.
Common trap — automated rollback on CloudWatch alarms via CodeDeploy.
Common trap — manual rollback next business day.
Common trap — sSHing into prod to poke around.

Isolate — Isolate (security group quarantine) to stop spread, snapshot for forensics, then eradicate — the contain→investigate→eradicate sequence. Immediate deletion destroys evidence; waiting lets it spread; paying ransoms is never the answer.

sections.heading: High Availability & Recovery
items: DR tiers — the lower tiers (backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby) trade recovery speed for cost and can't hit near-zero. A queue between tiers with visibility timeout (redelivery) and DLQ (poison isolation) decouples the services so one slow dependency can't exha…
Active-active — multi-site active-active with Route 53 routing serves traffic from multiple regions simultaneously — near-zero RTO/RPO by design, at the highest cost.
Route — Route 53 failover routing with health checks detects the failure and shifts DNS automatically.
Cell-based — Cell-based architecture (shuffle sharding) partitions customers into independent cells so a bad config or failure affects only a fraction.
Common trap — cell-based architecture (shuffle sharding) to bound blast radius.
Common trap — a single region with bigger instances.
Common trap — hoping downstream recovers fast.
Common trap — RPO 0 for everything regardless of cost.
Regular restore testing proves backups actually work — an untested backup is just a hope. Assuming, annual testing, or relying on replication (which replicates corruption too) all fail the same way.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For SDLC Automation: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one IaC & Config Management lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
Recite the key Monitoring & Logging terms from the glossary aloud from memory.
